analytic.title: A Conditional Abortable Priority Ceiling Protocol for Real-time Systems with Mixed Tasks

div.p: Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) is a well-known synchroniiation protocol for hard real-time systems. However, it has a problem of ceiling blocking which imposes a great hindrance to real-time systems especially for those with mixed tasks. In this paper, a new protocol called the Conditional A bortable Priority Ceiling Protocol (CA-PCP) is proposed. It resolves the problem by incorporating a conditional abort scheme into PCP. The new protocol inherits all the desirable characteristics from PCP and Ceiling Abort Protocol (CAP) which is yet another modification on PCP. In the proposed CA-PCP, a silent period is defined to control the number of aborts. During the period, it is conditional abortable so as to make a balance between blocking and abort of the tasks ajvnamicallv based on the utilization of the systems in order to achieve a high schedulability. Performance study of the proposed protocol has been done through simulation. The performance results indicate that CA-PCP can significantly improve the performance of a system if the length of the abortable critical sections are well-chosen.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In a hard real-time system, all the tasks must be scheduled to meet their deadlines. Otherwise, it may result in a disaster. One of the well-known scheduling algorithms for hard real-time systems is the Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) [Sha90]. It is based on the Rate Monotonic Analysis (M) [Liu73] which is for scheduling of hard real-time periodic tasks in an uniprocessor system. In RMA, priorities are assigned to periodic tasks according to the period of the tasks. A task with a shorter period is assigned a higher priority. Liu and Layland [Liu73] have shown that RMA is optimal among all static priority assignments algorithms if the total processor utilization of n periodic tasks in a processor is less than or equal to n(2"" -1).

RMA has a problem in handling data synchronization as it assumes that all the tasks are independent. This assumption is not valid as it is commonly found tasks Joseph Kee-Yin Ng Department of Computing Studies Hong Kong Baptist University Hong Kong email: jng@comp.hkbu.edu.hk sharing the same critical sections and data structures. Due to this problem, priority inversion may occurs and the blocking is indefinite [Sha94]. PCP resolves the problem by reservation achieved by the definition ceiling priority for each critical section. In PCP, a task will not be allowed to enter a particular critical section if the critical section has been reserved for a higher priority task.

Although PCP is suitable for hard real-time systems, it is not suitable for real-time systems with tasks having different criticality. That means some of the tasks are hard real-time tasks and the others are soft real-time tasks. Also, PCP has the problem of ceiling blocking. In a mixed realtime system, this problem is more serious. It is a situation in which a medium priority task is blocked by a lower priority task which is in a critical section with a higher ceiling priority. For example, there exist three classes of tasks which are different in their criticality: highly, medium and low. A highly critical task is sharing a critical section with a low critical task. According to PCP, if a low critical task enters a critical section, the ceiling priority will be raised and all medium critical tasks will be affected and are not allowed to enter any critical section.

In [Taka94], the Ceiling Abort Protocol (CAP) is proposed to make PCP to be abortable with an attempt to improve the performance of medium priority tasks. In CAP, a higher priority task can abort a lower priority task if it is in an abortable critical section and the priority ceiling of the critical section is lower than the priority of the higher priority task. However, there is no mechanism to control the number of aborts. Sometimes, aborting a task may create more harms than benefits. If the utilization is already high, aborting a task increases the utilization and can firther reduce the schedulability of the scheduling algorithm.

To solve the problem of ceiling blocking in PCP and the problems in CAP, we propose a new protocol called Conditional Abortable Priority Ceiling Protocol (CA-PCP) in which a condition is defined to assign the length of abortable critical section and the priority ceiling of each 0-8186-8034-2/97 $10.00 0 1997 IEEE section. The remaining parts of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the hard real-time scheduling algorithms: PCP and CAP. Section 3 defines CA-PCP. Section 4 describes the simulation model and its parameters. Section 5 summarizes the important performance results of CA-PCP. Finally, a conclusion of the paper is presented in Section 6 .

div.head: Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP)
div.p: The two major problems with priority scheduling with RMA due to data synchronization are deadlocks and priority inversion. Deadlocks are fatal in real-time systems because no tasks involved in a deadlock can complete in time. Priority inversion is a state of a system in which a higher priority task is forced to wait for a lower priority task. The reason for occurrences of priority inversion is that a low priority task may lock a critical section before a high priority task needs it. Uncontrolled priority inversion causes unpredictable delay for tasks. Utilizing the idea of priority ceiling for critical section, Priori@ Ceiling Protocol (PCP) integrates the scheduling algorithm with concurrency control protocol for task scheduling in hard real-time systems. With PCP, deadlocks are avoided and priority inversion delay is limited to at most the duration of a single critical section. The assumptions and definitions for PCP are summarized as follows:

1. Each task is scheduled according to RMA. 2. Critical sections are guarded by semaphores. 3. A priority ceiling c(S) is defined for each semaphore, S. c(S) is defined as the highest priority of the tasks which may access S. 4. Let S* be the semaphore with the highest priority ceiling of all semaphores currently locked by all other jobs. Before task J enters its critical section, it must first lock the semaphores S guarding the critical section. J will be blocked and cannot lock S if the priority of J, P(J, is not higher than the priority ceiling of semaphore S*, c(S*). In this case, J is said to be blocked on S* by the task which is holding the lock on S*. Otherwise, J will obtain the lock on Sand enter its critical section. 5. When task, J, exits its critical section, the semaphore associated with the critical section will be unlocked and the highest priority job, if any, blocked by J will be awakened.
6 . If task J blocks higher priority jobs, J inherits P,, the highest priority of the task blocked by J. When J exits a critical section, it resumes its original priority.

div.head: Conditional Abortable PCP (CA-PCP) 3.1 Definition
div.p: In this section, we define a new protocol called the Conditional Abortable Priority Ceiling Protocol (CA-PCP) which is based on PCP and CAP. CA-PCP is aimed for the real-time systems with mixed tasks which have different criticality. In this kind of systems, the problem of ceiling blocking is especially serious. In order to resolve the problem of ceiling blocking, it is abortable. However, it is conditional and is dependent on the current system status. A lower task can be aborted by a higher priority task even it is in a critical section. Similar to CAP, a critical section, CS, is divided into two parts: abortable critical section and non-abortable critical section as shown in Figure 2. The major difference between CA-PCP and CAP is that in CA-PCP the condition for aborting a lower priority task J, in CSg is more restrictive and is not only dependent on c(CS; ) and the priority of the requesting task. It is also dependent on other factors such as utilization and the amount of resource spent on the lower priority task. These factors are important as aborting a task will increase the system workload and increase the probability of other tasks missing their deadlines.

To cater in these factors, we define a silent period which is the minimum period of time between two consecutive aborts. The purpose of defining silent period is to make the condition for abort to be dependent on the existing utilization which is one of the most important factors on the schedulability of a scheduling algorithm. Aborting a task will increase the utilization and reduce the schedulability of the algorithm. It is important to control the number of aborts and only allow those aborts which will not increase the probability of deadline missing. The calculation of the length of the silent period will be discussed in next sub-section.

div.head: Simulation Model and Parameters
div.p: In order to investigate the performance of CA-PCP, a number simulation experiments have been performed. Figure 3 depicts the simulation model of the system with CA-PCP. It consists of four components: a set of Task Generators, a Task Queue, a Processor, a set of mechanisms for the control of semaphores and system ceiling. Tasks are generated from the task generator and are sent to the Task Queue in which they are queued up based on their priorities. The scheduler selects the first task in the queue for using the CPU. The scheduling is preemptable. When a new task arrives, its priority will be compared with the priority of the currently executing task. The higher priority task will be assigned to use the CPU and the lower one will be put in the Task Queue. A task will be blocked if its priority is not higher than the priority ceiling or its requesting semaphore is using by another task which is in its non-abortable critical section.
The system is defined with 9 classes of tasks which are classified into 3 groupshigh, medium and low priority tasks. Each class of task has different attributes as shown in Table 1.

It should be noted that we are not going to simulate a particular real-time system. Instead, in the determination of the model parameters and model configuration, we aim at investigating the performance characteristics of our proposed protocol and to compare its performance with PCP protocols. Thus, we start with a simple setup in which the system consists only a few semaphores so that it will have a high probability of semaphore conflict and a high chance of ceiling blocking. It is also assumed that high priority tasks have very short deadlines and low priority tasks have relatively longer deadlines.

The primary performance measure used is the number of deadline missing for each class of tasks. We also measure the mean CPU queue length which is an indicator on the degree of contention in the system. In order to investigate the impact of the length of abortable critical section on its performance, we define abortable critical section length (ACSL) as the length of abortable critical section over the length of non-abortable critical section.
The same value of ACSL will be assigned to all semaphores in the system.

div.head: Simulation Results and Analysis
div.p: The main difference between PCP and CA-PCP is that CA-PCP is abortable. It is expected that the larger the ACSL, the probability of aborts is higher. If the value of ACSL is zero, the protocol becomes PCP. Three important factors on the protocol performance are : (1) utilization; (2) probability of conflict in using the critical sections and the value of ACSL. Two set of experiments have be performed to study these factors on the performance of CA-PCP. One is on a high semaphore conflict probability environment and the other is on a medium semaphore conflict probability environment. For low semaphore conflict probability environment, the performance of CA-PCP should be similar to PCP as the probability of conflict is small. For the simulation of high semaphore conflict probability environment, a single semaphore is defined to pretend the case that many tasks accessing the same critical section which is guarded by the semaphore. For the simulation of medium semaphore conflict probability environment, the system attributes are following those defined in Table 1.

div.head: High Semaphore Conflict Probability
div.p: Figure 4 depicts the impact of ACSL on the performance of each class of tasks under 70% utilization and high semaphore conflict probability. It can be seen that when the value of ACSL is small (i.e., less than or equal to 0.4), the number deadline missing of the higher priority tasks (i.e., class 1 and class 2) is much higher than the number of deadline missing of the lower priority tasks. It is because the higher priority tasks have tighter deadline constraints and small value of ACSL means more ceiling blocking. When ACSL is equal to zero, the performance of the CA-PCP will be the same as PCP. Increasing the value of ACSL, the number of deadline missing of the higher priority tasks decreases. On the contrary, the number of deadline missing of the lower priority tasks increases. It is because increasing the value of ACSL increases the number of abort and the blocking of higher priority tasks will become smaller and shorter. At the same time, aborting tasks increases the utilization. Higher utilization gives lesser slack times for re-execution of the aborted tasks and for execution of lower priority tasks. Thus, the lower priority tasks have higher probabilities to miss their deadlines.

Figure 5 shows the total number of deadline missing of all the tasks under different utilization. For all utilization, increasing ACSL from small values, the total number of deadline missing decreases. When the value of ACSL is greater than certain value (i.e., ACSL = 0.6), the number of deadline missing starts to increase especially for high utilization ( >70%). When the utilization is low (< 70%), an increase in the value of ACSL can reduce the number deadline missing as the system has sufficient slack time for the aborted tasks to re-execute their aborted critical sections. When the utilization is high (> 70%), larger number of abort due to greater value of ACSL will increase the system workload. Therefore, more number of deadline missing will occur. From the above results, we can see that utilization has a very important impact on the performance of the protocol.

Figure 6 depicts the mean queue length of the system under different utilization. Increasing the value of ACSL can reduce the probability of semaphore conflict as the probability of a lower priority task holding a semaphore required by a higher priority task will become smaller. However, it also has an undesirable effect of higher system workload. So, the curves decreases slightly first from small value of ACSL. When the number of abort is high, the effect of re-execution of aborted tasks becomes dominant and the mean queue length increases gradually especially under high utilization.

div.head: Medium Semaphore Conflict Probability
div.p: Figure 7 shows the total number of deadline missing of all the tasks under different utilization and medium semaphore conflict probability. The number of deadline missing is smaller than under high semaphore conflict probability as the number of blocking and aborts are smaller. Consistent with the results under high semaphore conflict probability, by adjusting the values of ACSL, the system performance can be improved. If ACSL is set to be zero, the number of deadline missing is high even when the utilization is not very high. This is the performance of PCP.

Increasing the values of ACSL from small values, the number deadline missing decreases effectively. Under this situation, aborting tasks is still beneficial to the whole system performance. When the values of ACSL is greater than 0.6, the number of deadline missing increases. It is because there are too many aborts and the system does not have sufficient slack to handle them. When U = 90%, the minimum number of deadline missing occurs at larger values of ACSL.

Figure 8 shows the mean queue length under different utilization. It can be seen that it is about the same for different values of ACSL except when the utilization is very high (i.e., U = 90%). Although increasing the value of ACSL increases the number of abort, the system still has sufficient capacity to handle the additional workload as the existing utilization is not very high and the number of abort is not very high under medium semaphore conflict probability.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP), which is based on the Rate Monotonic Analysis ( M A ) , can solve two major problems in hard real-time systems: deadlock and priority inversion. However, it introduces a new problem called ceiling blocking which is especially serious for systems with mixed tasks. Although Ceiling Abortable Protocol (CAP) can solve part of the ceiling blocking problem, it has the problem of uncontrollable abort and it is difficult to determine the priority and the length of the abortable critical section. In this paper, a new protocol called the Conditional Abortable Priority Ceiling Protocol (CA-PCP) is proposed for scheduling mixed tasks in a real-time system. The main difference between CA-PCP and CAP is that a condition is defmed in CA-PCP based on the existing system utilization to dynamically adjust the condition for abort.

The performance evaluation on the newly proposed CA-PCP has been done using simulation. The results indicate that CA-PCP protocol can give a better performance as compared with PCP especially when a well-chosen value of length of abortable critical section is used. To summarize our simulation results, CA-PCP can reduce the number of deadline missing effectively especially under medium data contention by introducing a conditional abortable scheme to PCP. The protocol is very much in favor of the system that has some tasks with very short deadlines. Moreover, conditional abort can effectively avoid deadline missing in such kind of tasks.
